rejected.title: Why Australians enlisted
card: In 1914 Australia had no conscription for overseas service, so no law could make a man fight abroad. Every man who joined the Australian Imperial Force (AIF) was a volunteer.
Many felt loyal to Britain. They thought of it as the mother country and believed Australia should help defend the Empire.
Others wanted adventure and a chance to see the world. The army also paid a steady wage, which mattered when jobs were hard to find.
Family, friends and neighbours could add pressure. Men who stayed home might be shamed, while mates often enlisted together.
rejected.remember: Australians chose to enlist for many reasons: loyalty, adventure, pay and social pressure.

a.q: Which statement about the men who joined the AIF in 1914 is correct?
opts: They volunteered, though some felt pressure to join
They were called up by law to serve overseas
They were chosen by ballot to fill army quotas
They were ordered to join by state governments
a.why: Every AIF soldier was a volunteer, and pressure from family and friends was one reason some chose to join. Being called up by law is wrong, because in 1914 no law could make a man serve overseas.
a.clue: Could any law make a man fight abroad in 1914?

b.q: Tom, a farm worker in South Australia, enlists in 1914 after his three mates sign up. He also likes the idea of travel. Which reason best explains his choice?
opts: Pressure from friends and a sense of adventure
A legal duty to serve overseas
Loyalty to Britain and a wish for steady pay
A government order to leave farm work
b.why: The scenario names mates who enlisted and a wish to travel. These match social pressure and adventure. Loyalty and pay were real reasons for others, but nothing in Tom's story points to them.
b.clue: Look only at the reasons the story gives for Tom.
